content:
Whitney's reference is a short section of copy. It is a three-part "before you can..." sequence addressed to the reader as "you", and it is about the strategy that has to exist before ads run. Candidate B follows that structure closely. It keeps the three parallel sentences, with small shifts to "we" and "their". The "we" framing is slightly off from her "you" address, and the photographer/venue example is an addition. Even so, B is close to the reference in substance and format. Candidate A is a full email. It follows the original request, with the opener, the questions, the key lines and the 47 videos contrast. But the reference is only a three-sentence passage. If Whitney was working on that specific section, A would need heavy cutting. A also contains no "before you can..." structure, so the reference's core idea is only partly there. On substance, A has a lot that Whitney didn't include, though it matches the original request well. The comparison is against what she approved, and B is much closer to it. B needs only small edits: switching "we" to "you" and removing the extra detail. A would need major restructuring to reach the reference.
{"winner": "B", "edits_needed_A": "many", "edits_needed_B": "few", "reason": "Candidate B closely mirrors the approved three-part 'before you can...' structure and message, needing only pronoun and detail tweaks. Candidate A is a full email that doesn't contain the approved passage and would need heavy restructuring to match."}

request.system:
You compare two draft pieces of marketing copy for Wedding Industry Ads (WIA), a wedding-industry advertising agency. You are given the request, the version WIA's co-founder Whitney actually approved or wrote (the reference), and two candidate drafts. Decide which candidate would need fewer and smaller edits to become something Whitney would approve. Judge substance first (what is claimed, for whom, how WIA is positioned, accuracy, whether her own wording was kept where she supplied it), then voice. Do not reward length, and do not require the candidate to copy the reference wording.

Return only JSON: {"winner": "A" or "B" or "tie", "edits_needed_A": "few", "edits_needed_B": "many", "reason": "one or two sentences"} where edits_needed values are none, few, some or many.
request.user:
Request:
I want to continue working on a marketing email for Wedding Industry Ads. Please use an **editable Writing Block** for the email so I can edit the copy directly in ChatGPT.

**Context:**

This morning I taught a training inside The VAULT for members of our Google Ads and Meta Ads Accelerators about **Defining Your Unique Value Proposition (UVP).**

I don't want to turn the UVP workshop itself into marketing content or regurgitate the training. Instead, I want to use it as a behind-the-scenes example of the **depth of the work we do inside the Accelerators**.

The larger marketing idea we've identified is that advertising doesn't begin inside Google Ads or Meta Ads Manager. Before we can create strong ads and landing pages, we need to understand why the right client should care about and choose that particular business.

We also decided that I **do NOT want to lead with "If you don't know your UVP, you shouldn't be running ads."** That could accidentally imply prospects need to figure out their UVP before joining us. The stronger message is that **they don't need to have this figured out already because this is part of the strategic work we do with them inside the Accelerators.**

The email should begin with:

**"I taught a training this morning that technically had nothing to do with running ads."**

The story is that instead of talking about targeting, keywords, or campaign settings, we spent the workshop defining their UVPs and working through questions like:

-  Who are you particularly well suited to serve? 
-  What are those clients really trying to create through their wedding? 
-  What do you do especially well that actually matters to them? 
-  Which things you've been calling "differentiators" are meaningful reasons to choose you, and which could be said by 20 competitors? 

One of the central lines we liked was:

**"This is the part of advertising that doesn't happen inside the ad platform."**

From there, the email should naturally transition into why our Accelerators are different from an online course. We're not simply teaching wedding pros where to click inside Ads Manager. We help them develop the strategy underneath the ads, clarify their messaging, build their initial campaigns, understand the data, and learn how to make decisions from it.

Another idea we liked:

**"You're building an advertising system around your business, with someone beside you who knows what that system needs to look like."**

We also liked the concept of contrasting the Accelerator experience with buying a course that leaves someone with **"47 videos and a blank Ads Manager staring back at you."**

**Voice/style:** Write in Whitney's founder voice for Wedding Industry Ads. Conversational, confident, insightful, specific, and genuinely human. Avoid generic AI marketing language, em dashes, "it's not X, it's Y" constructions, overly punchy one-line copy for the sake of punchiness, and cliché marketing language.

Keep in mind the content and sales frameworks we've been using from our marketing consultant Savannah Jordan: founder POV, behind-the-scenes/process content, demonstrating the depth of the methodology rather than simply claiming expertise, and using the content to create demand for the offer.

**Please start by putting the current email draft into an editable Writing Block. Do not substantially rewrite it yet. I want to edit it with you from there.**

Reference (what Whitney approved):
Before you can write an ad that makes someone stop scrolling, you need to be able to articulate why they should care.
Before you can build a landing page that turns traffic into inquiries, you need to have clarity on what your ideal client actually wants and which parts of your business matter most to them.
And before you start paying to show up in a Google search or the Instagram newsfeed, you need to clearly give couples a reason to choose *your* business.

Candidate A:
:::writing{id="73184" variant="email" subject="The work that happens before we build your ads"}
I taught a training this morning that technically had nothing to do with running ads.

We were inside The VAULT with members of our Google Ads and Meta Ads Accelerators. And instead of talking about targeting, keywords, or campaign settings, we spent the workshop defining their unique value propositions.

Who are you particularly well suited to serve? What are those clients really trying to create through their wedding? What do you do especially well that actually matters to them?

And which things you’ve been calling “differentiators” are meaningful reasons to choose you, versus things that could be said by 20 competitors?

These questions shape what we say in an ad and what we emphasize on a landing page. They help us give the right couples a compelling reason to inquire.

This is the part of advertising that doesn’t happen inside the ad platform.

You can have a beautiful brand, a strong reputation, and years of experience serving couples, and still benefit from working through how to communicate what makes your business worth choosing.

You don’t need to have all of that figured out before joining us. It’s part of the work we do together inside the Accelerators.

And it’s one of the reasons the experience goes so much deeper than an online course.

We help you develop the strategy underneath your ads, clarify your messaging, and build your initial campaigns. Then we guide you as you learn to manage them, understand the data, and make decisions from it.

You’re building an advertising system around your business, with someone beside you who knows what that system needs to look like.

So when it’s time to put that strategy into practice, you have a campaign we’ve helped you launch and support as you learn. You’re never left with 47 videos and a blank Ads Manager staring back at you.

If you’ve been considering ads for your wedding business, what would you want help with first? Hit reply and let me know.

Whitney
:::

Candidate B:
Before we can write an ad that makes someone stop scrolling, we need to know why they should care.
Before we can build a landing page that turns traffic into inquiries, we need to understand what their ideal client actually wants and which parts of their business matter most to them.
And before we can put a photographer or venue in front of someone actively searching Google alongside a dozen competitors, we need to give that person a reason to choose *this* business.
